strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/8fabe0a5656e4311901671b8ca4248ce/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a relevant problem: parameter- and communication-efficient personalization of vision-language models under federated heterogeneity.
The separation into client-specific up/down projections and a globally aggregated shared projection is simple, intuitive, and easy to implement.
The local/base/novel evaluation attempts to measure personalization and generalization separately rather than reporting only aggregate accuracy.

The empirical study covers several classification datasets, label-skew regimes, multi-domain data, partial participation, and two CLIP backbones, with strong reported results on CIFAR and the domain-shift benchmark.
The paper is generally readable, and the architecture and communication flow are illustrated clearly.
weaknesses: The principal technical contribution is incremental: it combines the existing MMA adapter architecture with a standard shared-versus-personalized parameter decomposition. There is no theoretical analysis or substantial new optimization mechanism.

The experiments lack the ablations needed to validate the central design. Essential comparisons include aggregating the entire adapter, keeping the entire adapter local, federating only modality-specific components, removing the shared projection, varying the insertion layers and bottleneck size, and comparing modality-shared versus separate middle projections.

The baseline selection does not isolate the source of improvement. Nearly all principal baselines are prompt-based, while the proposed method uses adapters; there is no federated MMA baseline or other adapter/LoRA-based personalized FL baseline with matched trainable parameters and tuning budgets. Thus the results may demonstrate an advantage of adapters rather than of the proposed personalization scheme.

The communication-efficiency claim is unsupported by parameter counts, transmitted bytes per round, total communication, computation, memory, or wall-clock measurements. It is also unclear whether the communicated adapter is actually smaller than the prompts used by the baselines.

There are serious protocol inconsistencies. The abstract claims eleven datasets, the setup claims nine, and Table 1 reports seven while introducing OxfordPets without describing it in the dataset section. DomainNet has six domains and Office-Caltech10 four, so two clients per domain imply 12 and 8 clients respectively; Section 5.2 reverses these counts.

The purported domain-generalization experiment does not hold out domains: all domains participate in training and evaluation. It therefore measures performance under domain heterogeneity, not generalization to unseen domains. The very low CLIP accuracies in Table 2 also require a clearer explanation of the label space and evaluation protocol.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The text repeatedly refers readers to an appendix, but the submitted manuscript ends after the references and contains no appendix. Important details such as exact few-shot sample counts, base/novel splits, adapter insertion layer, optimizer settings, per-baseline hyperparameters, model-selection procedure, and complete partition construction are missing.

Statistical evidence is weak. Only Table 1 states that results are averaged over three seeds, no variance or confidence intervals are given, and some headline improvements are small enough that significance cannot be assessed. Tables 2 and 3 do not specify repeated runs.

The server uses an unweighted arithmetic mean in Eq. 11 despite potentially unequal client sizes induced by Dirichlet partitioning, whereas the preliminaries motivate data-size weighting. This choice is neither justified nor ablated, and behavior with partial client participation and stale personalized components is underspecified.

The claim of cross-modal information exchange is stronger than the formulation supports: the two branches apply the same projection weights independently, without directly mixing visual and textual features. The manuscript needs a more precise explanation or evidence that shared weights produce the claimed alignment.

Several conclusions overstate the evidence, including consistent superiority, scalability to real deployments, and privacy-sensitive applicability. No privacy attack analysis, differential privacy, secure aggregation, large-model scaling study, or deployment evaluation is provided. Overall, the promising results do not overcome the missing controls, protocol ambiguities, and reproducibility problems required for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: parameter-efficient personalization of vision-language models under federated data heterogeneity.
The proposed separation into client-specific up/down projections and a globally aggregated shared projection is intuitive and straightforward to implement.
The base-to-novel experiments cover several classification datasets and report local, base, and novel-class accuracy, exposing the personalization–generalization trade-off.
The method obtains strong reported results, including the highest average harmonic mean in the base-to-novel evaluation and improvements on CIFAR-10/100.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: pFedMMA largely combines the existing MMA adapter architecture with a standard partial-parameter personalization scheme, without a new learning objective, aggregation rule, or substantive technical analysis.

The baseline comparison is inadequate for establishing the central contribution. All principal competitors are prompt-based; the paper omits federated adapter/LoRA alternatives, local-only and globally aggregated MMA, standard partial-sharing PFL methods, and centralized MMA reference points. Consequently, the results cannot show that the proposed sharing strategy is preferable to obvious adapter-based alternatives.

No ablations isolate the contribution of the shared projection or asymmetric parameter sharing. Essential comparisons such as sharing all adapter parameters, sharing only up/down projections, using independent modality projections, changing insertion depth or bottleneck size, and removing federation are absent.

The communication-efficiency and scalability claims are unsupported: the paper reports no trainable-parameter counts, transmitted bytes, communication ratios, runtime, memory use, or comparison against baseline communication costs.

The experimental specification contains numerous contradictions. The abstract claims eleven datasets, Section 5.1 says nine, the listed CLIP datasets omit OxfordPets although Table 1 contains seven, and the reported DomainNet/Office-Caltech client counts are reversed between Sections 5.1 and 5.2. Figure 2 also states a common two-local-epoch setup despite CIFAR being described as using one local epoch.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript repeatedly refers readers to an appendix for dataset configurations and implementation details, but the submitted PDF has no appendix. It also omits crucial information including exact class splits, shot counts, preprocessing, initialization, optimizer details beyond learning rate, baseline-specific hyperparameters, validation/model-selection procedures, and aggregation/evaluation weighting.

The domain-shift results raise unresolved validity concerns. Zero-shot CLIP is near chance even on the 10-class Office-Caltech benchmark, yet the paper neither explains this surprising behavior nor supplies uncertainty estimates, repeated-run statistics, or sanity checks. Table 2 pools ten domains into one average despite the datasets having very different class spaces and difficulties.

Statistical support is incomplete. Only Table 1 mentions three seeds, no standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported, and Tables 2–3 and the learning curves do not state whether they are replicated. Many conclusions therefore rest on point estimates.

The empirical claims are overstated: the experiments concern image classification with CLIP rather than broader vision-language tasks, all domain identities appear during training, and only two backbones are mentioned while results are effectively presented for one. This does not substantiate broad claims about multimodal federated generalization or real-world scalability.

The presentation needs substantial correction, including inconsistent equations and terminology, equal rather than stated data-size-weighted aggregation, duplicated citations for FedPGP, typographical errors, and several inaccurate descriptions of the reported tables. Overall, the promising intuition is not supported with the rigor needed for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: balancing personalization, generalization, and communication cost when adapting vision-language models to heterogeneous federated data. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/4b5465aa7ef74c618471933a2a00a09c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The decomposition into client-specific up/down projections and a globally aggregated shared projection is simple, intuitive, and easy to implement while keeping the CLIP backbone frozen.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering base-to-novel transfer, pathological class partitions, Dirichlet label skew, and feature/domain heterogeneity. The reported average results are promising, especially for novel-class accuracy, CIFAR-100, and the combined DomainNet/Office-Caltech10 evaluation.
The paper is generally well organized, and the architecture and federated training procedure are described clearly enough to understand the main idea.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is modest: the architecture is largely inherited from the existing MMA adapter, while the principal new mechanism is assigning some adapter matrices to local training and one matrix to federated averaging. There is neither theoretical analysis nor deeper technical justification establishing why this particular partition is preferable.

The paper contains no meaningful ablation study. It does not compare alternative local/shared component assignments, fully shared MMA, entirely local MMA, unimodal adapters, different insertion depths, or bottleneck dimensions. Consequently, the central claim that the asymmetric decomposition causes the personalization-generalization trade-off is insufficiently supported.

The baseline set is incomplete and potentially favors the proposed approach: all substantive competitors are prompt-learning methods. Missing comparisons include federated MMA or adapter averaging, federated LoRA, local-only and centralized MMA, and standard partial-personalization methods. Parameter counts, computation, memory, and transmitted bytes are also absent, leaving the communication-efficiency and scalability claims unverified.

The claimed domain generalization evidence is not convincing because every domain participates in both training and evaluation; this tests performance under domain heterogeneity rather than generalization to an unseen domain. Results should include held-out-domain protocols and separate averages for DomainNet and Office-Caltech10.

Reproducibility and reporting have significant gaps. The text refers repeatedly to an Appendix that is not present, omits important details such as the adapter starting layer and exact data/class splits, and reports no variability for Tables 2 and 3. There are also contradictions: the paper alternately claims nine and eleven datasets, omits OxfordPets from the setup despite reporting it, and reverses the DomainNet/Office-Caltech10 client counts between Sections 5.1 and 5.2.

Although the results are promising, several gains are driven by very large improvements on a subset of domains, while the method loses on others. Without uncertainty estimates, matched-capacity baselines, or diagnostic ablations, the evidence is not yet strong enough for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: balancing personalization, out-of-client generalization, and communication cost when adapting vision-language models in federated settings.
The shared-versus-client-specific decomposition is intuitive: modality-specific up/down projections remain local, while a small cross-modal projection is aggregated.
The empirical scope is broad, covering eleven benchmarks, multiple shot counts, two CLIP backbones, label and domain shifts, and several recent federated prompt-learning baselines.
The method obtains strong average harmonic-mean accuracy in the principal base-to-novel experiments and communicates fewer parameters per round than the compared prompt methods.
The appendix provides useful implementation, ablation, learning-curve, and computational-cost information.
weaknesses: The central novelty is limited. The multi-modal adapter is inherited from prior MMA work, while retaining some parameters locally and aggregating another subset is a well-established personalized-FL strategy. The paper does not provide deeper technical analysis explaining why the shared middle projection is uniquely appropriate.

The comparisons do not isolate the benefit of the proposed federated decomposition from the benefit of replacing prompts with a substantially more expressive adapter. pFedMMA trains 248,832 parameters versus 8,192–74,240 for the baselines. Essential controls such as FedAvg-MMA, fully local MMA, and established partial-personalization adapter methods should be evaluated comprehensively using local, base, novel, and HM metrics.

The sharing-strategy ablation is incomplete: the main-text variants are reported only for local accuracy on four datasets, while the local-only comparison reports base/novel results without local accuracy or HM. Consequently, the evidence does not directly establish that the proposed split gives the claimed personalization-generalization trade-off.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. The manuscript appears to use a common optimizer and learning rate for all methods, but does not state whether each baseline was tuned according to its original protocol. The exceptionally poor generalization of some strong baselines makes this omission consequential.

Results are averaged over three seeds but no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. Some claimed gains are very small, including 0.05–0.23 percentage points on several CIFAR settings and 0.62 points on Office-Caltech10, so superiority is not established statistically.

Hyperparameters such as scaling factor, adapter dimension, and insertion depth appear to be selected from reported benchmark performance, but the paper does not describe a validation protocol. This raises the possibility of test-set-guided model selection.

There are important reproducibility and consistency problems: no code or precise configuration details are provided for every baseline; the client counts for DomainNet and Office-Caltech10 are swapped in Table 6 relative to the text; and Algorithm 1 selects a subset of clients but aggregates with a sum over all N clients and a 1/N factor rather than over the selected set.

The communication-efficiency claim is too broad. Although per-round transmitted parameter count is low, pFedMMA has the largest trainable parameter count, longer training time than several baselines, and the paper does not analyze total communication over convergence, communication in bytes, client storage, or heterogeneous-device constraints.

The presentation contains numerous grammatical, formatting, and citation defects, and several dense tables and plots are difficult to read. Overall, the promising empirical results do not overcome the incremental contribution and evaluation gaps required for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: communication-efficient personalization of vision-language models under federated data heterogeneity.
The shared/local adapter decomposition is intuitive: modality-specific projections remain personalized while a small cross-modal projection is federated.
The empirical scope is broad, covering eleven datasets, label and feature shifts, two CLIP backbones, multiple few-shot regimes, and several recent federated prompt-learning baselines.

Reported results are promising: pFedMMA generally improves the aggregate harmonic mean of local, base, and novel-class accuracy, and the appendix includes useful communication, runtime, memory, and design-ablation analyses.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The work largely combines the existing MMA architecture with a standard shared-versus-local parameter decomposition and FedAvg-style aggregation; there is little new technical analysis explaining why the shared middle projection should provide the claimed generalization.

The central comparisons are not adequately controlled. pFedMMA trains roughly 249K parameters, versus 8K–74K for the prompt baselines, so its gains may reflect substantially greater adaptation capacity rather than the proposed sharing strategy. Parameter-matched adapter baselines and established personalized-FL algorithms applied to the same MMA architecture are missing.

The sharing ablations do not repair this concern: the all-global and reversed-sharing variants report only local accuracy on four datasets, while the local-only comparison reports only base/novel accuracy. Full local/base/novel/HM results under identical hyperparameters are needed for all variants.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates or statistical tests despite reporting averages over three seeds. Several headline improvements are small, including many CIFAR gains below one percentage point, so their significance cannot be assessed.

Experimental reproducibility and fairness are insufficiently documented. There is no stated code release, and important details such as exact class/client partitions, adapter initialization, optimizer momentum and regularization, seed identities, baseline-specific tuning, and hyperparameter-selection protocol are absent. It is unclear whether hyperparameters were selected using the reported test benchmarks.

There are consequential internal inconsistencies. Table 6 reverses the DomainNet and Office-Caltech10 client counts relative to the main text, the aggregation equations divide by N even when only a subset of clients participates rather than clearly using participating-client or sample-size weights, and Algorithm 1 contains inconsistent return indices. These issues undermine confidence in the exact implementation.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. Communication is low, but pFedMMA has the largest trainable parameter count and is neither the fastest nor the lowest-memory method; consequently, calling it broadly efficient or scalable is not established. Likewise, the experiments are simulations on standard classification datasets and do not substantiate real-world federated deployment claims.

Presentation quality needs improvement: several tables are extremely dense, there are numerous grammatical and typographical errors, citation metadata is incomplete or duplicated, and terminology such as “baseline/non-baseline” is used inconsistently. Overall, the promising empirical signal is not supported by sufficiently rigorous, controlled, and reproducible evidence for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant approach: modality-specific adapter projections remain personalized while a compact cross-modal projection is federated. This is simple, intuitive, and communication-efficient.
The evaluation is broad, covering eleven datasets, label and feature heterogeneity, base-to-novel transfer, multiple shot counts, two CLIP backbones, and up to 100 clients.

Results provide concrete positive evidence: pFedMMA generally achieves the best balance among local, base, and novel accuracy, and performs especially well under severe non-IID CIFAR partitions and on DomainNet.

The adapter-sharing, bottleneck-dimension, insertion-layer, and scaling-factor ablations support important design choices. The cost analysis also shows that only 3,072 parameters per client direction are communicated per round for the reported ViT-B/16 configuration.
The method and training procedure are presented clearly, and the appendices contain substantial per-dataset results and implementation details.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. The architecture is inherited from an existing multi-modal adapter, while retaining client-specific layers and aggregating a shared layer follows a well-established personalized-FL decomposition. The claimed first use in this setting is useful but not, by itself, a major methodological advance.

The headline advantage on the main 16-shot benchmark is modest against the strongest actual comparator: average harmonic-mean accuracy is 84.15 versus 83.09 for PromptFL. The reported 6.4% improvement instead excludes PromptFL and compares against FedPGP, which makes the gain appear stronger than the complete baseline set supports. pFedMMA also loses to PromptFL on several individual settings.

Although experiments are reportedly repeated three times, no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. This is important because several improvements are below one percentage point.

Baseline fairness and hyperparameter selection are insufficiently documented. pFedMMA trains substantially more local parameters than the prompt methods, and the paper does not explain comparable tuning budgets or how scaling factors and insertion layers were selected without using test performance.

The domain-shift evaluation uses only ten selected DomainNet classes rather than the full benchmark, produces unusually low baseline accuracies, and shows only a small Office-Caltech10 average gain. This weakens the broad real-world robustness claim.

There are reproducibility and consistency issues: no code-release statement is provided; baseline configurations are incomplete; Table 6 swaps the stated client counts for DomainNet and Office-Caltech10; and the algorithm averages by N despite partial participation, rather than clearly using the selected-client count or data-size weights.

Claims about scalability and real-world federated deployment are stronger than the evidence: the study is simulated, provides no privacy or adversarial analysis, and does not evaluate heterogeneous devices, client dropout, or substantially larger federations.
